items.title: IFLA endorses International Science Council definition of the Right to Science
items.raw_text: Despite appearing in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the right to science – both to participate in and benefit from science – too often does not enjoy the same profile as other rights. Yet the costs of failing to uphold this are significant, not just in terms of academics’ own ability to pursue their work free from undue pressures from governments and others, but also in the quality, accessibility and usability of research outputs by the wider population. Politically motivated cuts, bans on addressing certain topics, the withdrawal of access to key resources, the blocking or defunding of international cooperation, the incompleteness of the drive towards open access, and underinvestment in citizen science and science communication – all put into question the right to science. In order to consolidate efforts by the community in order to resist these trends, and promote this right as both a goal in itself and an enabler of so many other goals, the International Science Council (of which IFLA is a member and partner) has developed a definition of the Right to Science . This expands on what is present in the Universal Declaration, but remains accessible. It condenses down much existing work, including at the UN Human Rights Council as well, as well as taking account of the need also for responsibility in science, not least in implementing the CARE principles when working with Indigenous communities. The webinar explored how researchers can think beyond individual technical tools and consider the broader methodological context surrounding qualitative analysis. It also examined qualitative research across disciplines, including education, social sciences, engineering and health sciences, with particular attention to the challenges researchers face when deciding how to analyze qualitative data. Hagman emphasized that qualitative research has “too many meanings,” offering researchers considerable freedom but also requiring them to explain and justify the choices they make. items.title: Refreshing for the Future
items.raw_text: Library renovations can feel overwhelming—especially when you’re juggling tight budgets, big community expectations, and a building that’s showing its age. The good news is you don’t have to choose between “do nothing” and “tear it down.” Most successful library upgrades live somewhere in the middle: a smart, phased plan that protects your long-term vision while making meaningful improvements right now. Here are a few practical ways to think about approaching a library renovation: Start with a North Star. Before you pick finishes or start talking timelines, take a step back and get clarity on what you want your library to become. I call this the north star —your vision for how the building should function for staff and the public. Even if you only have funding for part of the work today, guiding principles help you avoid spending money on changes you’ll undo later. Renovations are much easier when everyone can point to the same end goal—even if you’re getting there in phases. Assess the building first. It’s tempting to jump straight into visible improvements, but understanding existing conditions is what sets a project up for success. A solid facility-condition evaluation looks at the status of major building systems and flags components that may be nearing the end of their life cycle, such as mechanical systems, electrical panel capacity, and even finishes like carpet. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . items.title: Mall Wonder
items.raw_text: After serving its community for nearly 45 years in the same building, Escondido (Calif.) Public Library closed in April 2025 for an $11.6 million renovation. It was important to us, as the city’s lone library, to preserve access during construction. So one month later, our library opened a temporary location in a very different kind of facility: the nearby North County Mall, where services and collections were spread across six storefronts, including a former Abercrombie & Fitch clothing store. Of course, moving a library takes more than a month. Our planning took more than a year and required staff to work under tight deadlines, limited budgets, and high expectations. Here’s how we did it, and what we learned from the process. Choosing a location. It’s essential to consider whether the new location will match, improve upon, or limit access. Retailers and mall operators have already studied traffic patterns, visibility, parking, and nearby amenities. Leverage that knowledge to evaluate access. In our case, the public benefited from a highway and bus stop near the mall, and adjacency to a city park. The arrangement also gave the mall a stable civic tenant and created natural cross-traffic between library patrons and shoppers. The mall was not just available space; it was a location where public access, economic development, and community visibility could overlap. items.title: Dismantling Disinformation
items.raw_text: Library workers are well aware of the effects of book bans and censorship. Propaganda and disinformation are the flipside of the same coin. Understanding the complex relationships among these interrelated processes is more critical than ever, especially as libraries explore possible solutions and responses. The following books show how disinformation can lead to censorship and how censorship can, in turn, allow disinformation to thrive. Book Bans, Disinformation, and Cultural Erasure: The Censor­ship Movement in Libraries, Schools, and Society By Paul T. Jaeger Jaeger situates the current book-banning movement within a larger social and political effort to erase marginalized communities and culture. He provides clear definitions and examples of these processes and goals, including the roles played by technological progress and economic inequity. With accessible references (like the Beatles, Dungeons & Dragons, and Holmes and Watson) and nuanced examinations of McCarthyism, the history of libraries, and the myth of neutrality, this is a recommended read for anyone interested in a more expansive understanding of current First Amendment challenges. items.title: Elena, Aris, Marcus: : AI-Generated ‘Ghosts’ are Polluting the Scientific Literature
items.raw_text: From Nature: Elena Vasquez spent three months camping on the rim of Mount Nyiragongo in the Democratic Republic of the Congo back in 2019. She says the sulfur dioxide there smelt like “burnt matches mixed with rotten eggs”. Her colleague, Marcus Chen, has witnessed 11 volcanic eruptions across four continents. Vasquez and Chen’s accounts appeared on Volcanoes Explored, a now-defunct website that described itself as a resource for “exploring the dynamic world of volcanoes”. But there’s a problem: these tales are not real and the pair of volcanology specialists is made up. Vasquez and Chen are ‘ghost’ identities generated by Claude — the large language model (LLM) made by Anthropic in San Francisco — when prompted by users to create fictional experts, according to a preprint published in June. Gemini, Google’s LLM, was found to use a different pair of recurring characters, called Aris Thorne and Lena Petrova, and OpenAI’s GPT repeatedly used the name Elara Voss. [Clip] Fake experts such as these can be found across the Internet as everything from blockchain specialists and astronauts to board members and podcast hosts, and they raise specific concerns around integrity of the scientific literature, say Neo Christopher Chung and Michał Brzozowski, computer scientists at the Samsung AI Center Warsaw in Poland and co-authors of the preprint. items.title: Mellon Foundation Releases: “Mapping the Landscape of Community-Based Archives” Report
items.raw_text: From the Mellon Foundation: Today, the Mellon Foundation released “Powerful but Precarious: Mapping the Landscape of Community-Based Archives,” the first national study of its kind. Produced in partnership with research firm Engage R+D, the study draws on a survey of 336 independent, community-led archives, and in-depth interviews with more than 20 practitioners across the country. Community-based archives are independent organizations that collect and preserve the records, photographs, oral histories, personal papers, and other artifacts of communities many of which have been historically excluded from mainstream institutions. Unlike institutional archives, community-based archives often hold materials that exist nowhere else – collections that, if lost, cannot be recovered. Additionally, community-based archives often operate outside of the context of universities, libraries, historical societies, or other collecting institutions and in doing so, they serve as civic infrastructure where people can access and learn about their own localized or underexplored histories. While hundreds of these archives exist across the United States, serving communities of every background and geography, they have never been mapped, counted, or examined at this scale—leaving them largely invisible to the funders, policymakers, and organizations best positioned to support them. items.title: Report: Chinese-Owned Science Journal Created to Rival the Best
items.raw_text: From Nature: A new Chinese-owned journal has set its sights on rivalling the world’s oldest and most influential academic titles. Vita is one of several English-language journals that have launched in China in the past couple of years. They represent the country’s latest effort to create prestigious global journals, as part of the government’s Journal Excellence Action Plan, which began in 2019. [Clip] Vita is jointly funded by the Higher Education Press, a subsidiary of China’s Ministry of Education based in Beijing, and Westlake University in Hangzhou, its editorial team says. It publishes papers in biological sciences. Its first print issue came out in July. As an open-access journal, Vita waives article-processing charges (APCs), fees many publishers require authors to pay when publishing open access articles. [Clip] Vita ’s model is “clearly going to be appealing” to authors, says James Butcher, a former publisher who runs a consultancy firm called Journalology near Liverpool, UK. But he warns that keeping the model running in the long term will be a challenge for the journal and its funders because “publishing is expensive”. Publishers who charge APCs say that the money helps to cover the costs of publishing open access, including paying the salaries of in-house editors and production staff, as well as printing and server costs. Drawing on 771 responses, this year’s report provides an opportunity to look beyond a single snapshot and begin tracking how AI adoption, attitudes, policies, and concerns are changing over time. [Clip] An Industry Moving Toward More Structured AI Use One of the clearest changes from 2025 is happening at the organizational level. In 2026, 63% of respondents said their organization is using AI, up from 48% in 2025. Individual use moved in the opposite direction, falling from 46% to 38%. Organization size also matters: 88% of organizations with more than 100 employees reported using AI. Adoption does not necessarily mean unrestricted use. items.title: Report: Oxford Lets OpenAI Train Its AI Models On Historical Texts From the Bodleian Library
items.raw_text: From The Guardian: The University of Oxford has allowed the company behind ChatGPT to train its AI models on historical texts from its Bodleian Library, as tech companies scour academic institutions for fresh data. The Bodleian material digitised by OpenAI has been used to “populate the OpenAI training set”, according to internal documents. Oxford announced a partnership with the company in March 2025, using OpenAI software to digitise texts from the university’s world-famous library, which it said would make the content more widely available for students and researchers. However, the announcement did not state the material would be used for training OpenAI’s models, which are trained to recognise patterns in words – and thus “learn” to write complete sentences and perform other cognitive tasks – by being fed vast amounts of data. [Clip] Meeting minutes at the University of Oxford, obtained via a freedom of information request, record concerns from staff, including members of the Bodleian governance committee, about the reputational risk of partnering with OpenAI and the effect on the university’s environmental commitments of striking a deal involving an energy-intensive technology. items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. She reconnects with childhood friends and finds herself caught in a love triangle between her schoolgirl crush, Andre, and an intriguing new girl, India, who has just moved to her cousin’s neighborhood. items.title: Expanding Access Through Inclusive Collections
items.raw_text: Receiving a scholarship to attend PLA 2026 in Minneapolis gave me the opportunity to learn from innovative libraries and inspiring information professionals. One session in particular, “Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities,” presented by Plano Public Library and Libraries for All LLC, reinforced a simple but urgent idea: if members of our community cannot meaningfully use our materials, we are not fully meeting our mission. Access is about more than having a collection. It is about ensuring that everyone can engage with and benefit from it. The session highlighted how people with disabilities are often underserved by traditional library collections. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Some readers may have physical disabilities that make turning pages difficult. Others may benefit from visual supports, tactile elements, or alternative ways of interacting with a text. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. Before attending the session, my understanding of accessibility largely centered on traditional formats such as large print and braille. Learning about adaptive books expanded that perspective. items.title: Connections, Ideas, and a Little Hope: Reflections from PLA 2026
items.raw_text: I had the distinct honor of attending PLA 2026 in Minneapolis thanks to a PLA scholarship. As an eastern North Dakota native, Minneapolis is a familiar destination, but spending several days surrounded by thousands of energized library professionals made the city feel vibrant and new, despite the wind, cold, snow, and more wind. The connections, reunions, and conversations I experienced throughout the conference reminded me why gatherings like PLA matter. Alongside reconnecting with colleagues and making new professional connections, I left with fresh ideas, practical tools, and renewed optimism about the future of libraries. Several sessions stood out to me, both because of their content and because of the presenters who brought those ideas to life. One of the first sessions I attended was “Becoming One Library: How to Build Better Internal Communications,” presented by Mary Kapusta of Calgary Public Library. Kapusta was engaging, funny, honest, and refreshingly candid about both the successes and challenges of implementing a completely redesigned internal communications strategy across 23 library branches. What impressed me most was how scalable the ideas felt. Calgary Public Library serves nearly 1,000 employees, while my library employs roughly 30 staff members, yet many of the concepts felt immediately applicable. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books. Their team selected popular picture books, organized volunteer workshops to create adapted versions, trained staff to support the collection, and developed cataloging practices for these unique materials. items.title: Information Strategies for Libraries in the Age of AI
items.raw_text: Librarians must actively adapt to an information landscape increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), search engine optimization (SEO), and algorithm-driven content. During the PLA 2026 session, *”Trust & Verify: Information Accuracy in the Age of SEO, AI, and Algorithms,”* Nathaniel Burnard, Systems Services Manager at Allen County Public Library, offered a practical and timely examination of how these forces influence the way we, and our patrons, discover and evaluate information. As a 2026 PLA scholarship recipient, I had the opportunity to attend Burnard’s insightful presentation in Minneapolis. Burnard began by explaining the differences between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation (MDM). While these terms are often used interchangeably, they differ based on the intent behind the creation or sharing of information. Misinformation is false or inaccurate information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is deliberately false information created to manipulate, mislead, or cause harm. Malinformation contains truthful information that is presented in a misleading, sensationalized, or harmful way. To help identify MDM, Burnard encouraged attendees to ask critical questions such as, “Does this content provoke a strong emotional response?” and “Does it use small pieces of valid information that have been exaggerated or distorted?” He also emphasized the importance of avoiding engagement with misleading content.
